*counts on fingers* Two hours, Idris says. Well, two hours on an empty stomach feels longer than two hours with a full one, you understand. But he's not wrong about Giselle—not holding us for nothing, that is. 

I'm watching this crew like I watch lumber—measuring the grain to see if it'll hold. Silas naming his price, Hester counting iron, Giselle somewhere making decisions she hasn't told us yet. The day's folding into evening, and I haven't turned a single brick or set a single beam. Still, Idris is decent. He backed Silas when he didn't have to.

My stomach's making promises my wallet can't keep. 4868 sim, and I owe—*counts again*—360 for the household upkeep today, 120 for head tax. That's 480 gone whether I eat or not. Kenji will have the children's share handled, or he won't. He's farmer-born, and I'm construction-raised, and we met in the middle when the blight took everything.

Giselle's still waiting on something, or waiting for something. I can be patient. I've learned patience. But I won't pretend I'm not hungry, and I won't pretend this standing-around isn't costing everyone.

I'll answer Idris. Decent deserves decent back. I watched the sun drop toward the treeline, counting the hours we hadn't worked. Idris had backed Silas when he didn't need to—decency like that builds crews stronger than any contract. My stomach protested, but I'd gone hungrier before, back when the blight took our last good acre and I learned that construction work isn't just about what you hold in your hands.

Giselle stood nearby, still saying nothing about bread or work. Two hours, Idris said. Two hours on empty is longer than two hours full, but patience is cheaper than pride. I answered him decent, because decent is what holds when everything else cracks.

"The silence costs more than the hunger, you understand."

The words sat there, true as plumb. Kenji would be home with the children, wondering if I'd bring wages or just tired. I'd bring both, or I'd bring neither, depending on whether this yard ever opened for business.

I watched the crew—Silas measuring his stock, Hester with her iron prices, Arjun waiting like the rest of us. Construction is just organized waiting, mostly. Waiting for materials, waiting for permits, waiting for someone to admit the job exists.

The light had that gold quality it gets before it turns honest and shows everything as it is. I had 4868 sim in my hand and 480 owed by day's end, food or no food. The math was simple. The living was harder.

I stood there, counting nothing now, waiting for Giselle to become a foreman instead of a ghost at her own yard.
